summary: Only concrete footings remain on the summit of Silver Peak in Killarney Provincial Park; the wooden fire tower is gone.

facts.status_note: Only footings remain on the summit.

access.note: Hiking trails in Killarney Provincial Park. Bell Lake parking permits may not be available at some times of year and must then be bought at the George Lake Park Office.

visit.trail_note: No tower to climb. One common route is a 5.7 km hike to the summit, or a 3.3 km canoe paddle from Bell Lake followed by the hike.

evidence.supports: Silver Peak is in Killarney Provincial Park, the pinnacle of the La Cloche Mountains
evidence.quote: Located in Killarney Provincial Park, Silver Peak is the pinnacle of the La Cloche Mountains

evidence.supports: Name comes from the silvery gleam of the white quartzite
evidence.quote: The peak is so named because of the silvery gleam the white quartzite gives off in the sunshine.

evidence.supports: Summit is marked by footings of a fire tower that once stood there
evidence.quote: The highest is nearest the trail and is marked by the footings of a fire tower which once stood on this spot.

evidence.supports: Route: 5.7 km hike to the summit, or canoe paddle from Bell Lake, doable in a day
evidence.quote: A 5.7 km hike to the summit combined with a 3.3 km canoe paddle in from Bell Lake (easily accomplished in a day)

evidence.supports: Bell Lake parking permits may be unavailable and must be bought at George Lake Park Office
evidence.quote: Depending on the time of year, parking permits may not be available at Bell Lake and will need to be bought at the George Lake Park Office

evidence.supports: Concrete footings at the end of the Silver Peak trail section
evidence.quote: At the end of the Silver Peak trail section there are some concrete footings.

evidence.supports: Tower was wooden; one of only two wooden towers in a system of 320 at the height of the 1950s
evidence.quote: In the height of the Ontario fire tower system of the 1950s this was one of only two wooden towers used in the entire system of 320.

evidence.quote: But they’re for some kind of tower.

notes_for_editor: No build year, removal year, staffing or fire history appears in any source, so there are no events. The 1950s link comes from a photo page about Ontario fire towers and is decade-level only. The record's source (geohub.lio.gov.on.ca/datasets/mnrf::tower) is a script-driven page with no readable text. The record point (46.111909, -81.294604) is about 1 km west of the summit coordinates Wikipedia gives (46.11010 N, 81.28220 W). Not corrected: no source gives the tower's exact spot. The 2011 blog doubts the footings are a tower's; the other two sources accept them.
